@graph.headline: Recovery Factor: Was the Pain Worth It? (Net Profit ÷ Worst Drawdown, Honestly Explained)

mainEntity.name: What is recovery factor in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Net profit divided by maximum drawdown. The one-line answer: how many times your worst pain fits inside your profit. A recovery factor of 5 means you made five rupees for every rupee of worst drawdown you endured.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate recovery factor?

acceptedAnswer.text: RF = Net Profit ÷ Maximum Drawdown, using same-currency, same-period inputs. Net profit must be after costs, and the drawdown should be the worse of balance vs equity drawdown — equity includes open trades and is the harsher, truer number. Worked example: ₹4,20,000 net profit over 2 years with a worst drawdown of ₹84,000 gives RF = 5.0.

mainEntity.name: What is a good recovery factor?

acceptedAnswer.text: The honest band: below 1.0 is a red flag (the strategy hasn't recovered from its worst loss); ~1.6 is an old community stability floor; above 3 is the "worth considering" consensus; 2–5 is good; above 5 is very good; 10+ is excellent. Sources disagree on exact cutoffs, so treat the band as direction, not gospel. The retail takeaway: demand 3+ before serious money, and treat 5+ as the real comfort zone.

mainEntity.name: Recovery factor vs profit factor — what's the difference?

acceptedAnswer.text: Profit factor is gross profit ÷ gross loss: it measures win/loss efficiency and ignores the path. Recovery factor is net profit ÷ max drawdown: it measures pain efficiency. A strategy can have a beautiful profit factor of 2.0 while a 45% trough nearly killed the trader — profit factor doesn't price the scar; recovery factor does.

mainEntity.name: Recovery factor vs Calmar ratio — are they the same?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The recovery factor's numerator is the total net profit over the test period; the Calmar ratio's numerator is the annualized return. Both divide by maximum drawdown. That makes Calmar comparable across periods while recovery factor is not — never compare recovery factors across different test windows.

mainEntity.name: Why does recovery factor go up with longer backtests?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because profit accumulates roughly linearly with sample length while the maximum drawdown is one sticky event that mostly doesn't deepen. The numerator grows with every trade; the denominator stays fixed unless a new worst drawdown occurs. So a longer window inflates the ratio mechanically — the same system can score RF 2.1 on a 1-year window and 8.0 on a 5-year window. Compare recovery factors only across identical test windows.

mainEntity.name: Should you use balance drawdown or equity drawdown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use the worse of the two. Equity drawdown includes open trades and is the harsher, truer number — balance drawdown measures closed trades only. Computing recovery factor on balance drawdown flatters the system. If your platform reports both, take the larger one.

mainEntity.name: What does recovery factor NOT tell you?

acceptedAnswer.text: Recovery factor is a filter, not a verdict — and a validator, not an optimization target. Its four blind spots are time underwater (a 25% dip recovered in a week vs two years is the same RF but not the same strategy), profit concentration (one monster trade can inflate the numerator), live costs (a borderline backtest RF often dies in the real market), and ruin probability. It also inflates mechanically with longer backtests — never compare recovery factors across different test windows. ---
